transcript:
Fireflies.ai Meeting Transcript

Title: B200 performance bring-up + tuning recommendations (Redwood x NVIDIA)
Date: 2025-11-19
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 57 minutes
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees:
- Irene Choi (Redwood Inference)
- Isabella Rossi (Redwood Inference)
- Hiro Tanaka (Redwood Inference)
- Sofia Ivanova (Redwood Inference)
- Noah Patel (Redwood Inference)
- Rina Kobayashi (Redwood Inference)
- Anil Kumar (NVIDIA)
- Sarah Lin (NVIDIA)
- Marco DeLuca (NVIDIA)
- Priya Nair (NVIDIA)

Summary (auto-generated):
Redwood reviewed early B200 access constraints and asked NVIDIA for recommended driver/CUDA stack versions and tuning areas for LLM inference. NVIDIA highlighted differences vs H100, advised validating FP8/Transformer Engine paths, attention kernel selection behavior by sequence length, and multi-GPU collectives settings (NCCL). Redwood outlined the plan to ship a gated “experimental B200” hardware tuning profile pack with explicit rollback and perf canary gates.

Topics (auto-generated):
- B200 software stack (driver, CUDA, firmware) assumptions
- Kernel-selection guidance: attention/GEMM/FP8
- Scheduler and batching knobs for long context and streaming
- KV cache memory behavior and fragmentation observations
- NCCL / collectives defaults for multi-GPU and multi-node
- Operational guardrails: gating, compatibility checks, rollback

Questions (auto-generated):
- What are the minimum stable driver and CUDA versions for B200 LLM inference?
- Any known issues with long-context + FP8 paths on early B200 stacks?
- Recommended NCCL environment variables for NVLink/NVSwitch systems?
- How should profile selection behave with MIG/partitioned setups?

Transcript:

[00:00] Irene Choi (Redwood): Okay, I think we’re good. Thanks everyone for making time. This is our B200 bring-up deep dive. We have limited fleet access right now, so we’re trying to make sure our first pass is not, like, obviously wrong. We’ve shipped H100 and L40S presets already and want B200 behind an experimental gate.

[00:23] Sarah Lin (NVIDIA): Sounds good. Thanks for inviting us. Maybe quick round of intros? I’m Sarah, dev rel, mostly I help route questions to the right folks. Marco’s here from driver systems side, Priya from NCCL, and Anil from solutions.

[00:38] Isabella Rossi (Redwood): I’m Isabella, kernel microbench and new SKU tuning on Redwood’s runtime.

[00:44] Hiro Tanaka (Redwood): Hiro, I’m on kernel tuning lead, attention and GEMM paths.

[00:48] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): Sofia, scheduling and batching.

[00:51] Rina Kobayashi (Redwood): Rina, benchmark harness and workload matrix.

[00:55] Noah Patel (Redwood): Noah, runtime architecture and regression strategy.

[01:00] Irene Choi (Redwood): Great. So the agenda: we’ll give you our constraints, then ask about recommended stack and where you’ve seen perf go sideways in B200 bring-up. Then discuss multi-GPU/multi-node and NCCL defaults. And finally what we should document as “expected behavior” vs guarantees.

[01:19] Anil Kumar (NVIDIA): Works.

[01:20] Irene Choi (Redwood): Constraints: we’ve got a small number of B200 nodes, mixed configs. Some are SXM-ish and some are PCIe, and the naming strings are not consistent. Like nvidia-smi reports “NVIDIA B200” on one, and “B200-SXM5” on another. We’re normalizing detection strings in our loader.

[01:39] Marco DeLuca (NVIDIA): Yep, that’s common early on. You’re doing the right thing, normalize. Also check the PCI device ID if you can, that’s more stable.

[01:47] Noah Patel (Redwood): We do have access to device IDs, but we’ve historically preferred to keep it simple. For the profile loader we’ll probably do: SKU string normalize first, then fallback to device ID mapping if ambiguous.

[02:01] Marco DeLuca (NVIDIA): That’s a good plan. And if you’re in Kubernetes, sometimes the device plugin surfaces a different string than the bare host.

[02:10] Irene Choi (Redwood): Exactly. Okay, software stack. What’s your recommended minimum driver and CUDA for B200? Our infra is currently testing 55x drivers with CUDA 12.x. We’ve heard “12.4 or 12.5” thrown around.

[02:27] Marco DeLuca (NVIDIA): For B200, you want to be on a fairly recent R550 driver line. I can follow up with exact minimums we consider “production stable.” Generally, CUDA 12.4+ is the safe baseline. CUDA 12.5 has improvements but also depends on your container base.

[02:46] Isabella Rossi (Redwood): Is there anything specific where older 12.3 just breaks? Like missing kernels, or performance cliffs?

[02:53] Marco DeLuca (NVIDIA): Some of it is “supported but not optimal.” But I’d say you’ll miss some of the tuned kernels and you may see oddities in TE FP8 paths. Also we’ve seen a couple of issues with long-running jobs and memory reporting; those were fixed in later drivers.

[03:13] Hiro Tanaka (Redwood): So for us, the big question is which knobs should be pinned in a B200 profile. We’ve got kernel auto-select heuristics bucketed by sequence lengths (short vs medium vs long). For H100 that was very sensitive. Should we expect similar sensitivity on B200?

[03:35] Anil Kumar (NVIDIA): Yes, even more in some cases because the optimal kernel can change with sequence and batch shape, and also whether you’re doing FP16/BF16 or FP8. If you’re using FP8 heavily, pay attention to the matmul and attention kernels that are TE-backed.

[03:52] Hiro Tanaka (Redwood): Understood. We support BF16 broadly and we have an FP8 mode, but it’s not default for all models. For the initial “experimental B200” profile, we may keep FP8 disabled unless the model explicitly enables it.

[04:07] Sarah Lin (NVIDIA): That’s reasonable. You don’t want to flip precision defaults silently.

[04:12] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): From scheduler angle, we saw H100 respond well to slightly more aggressive continuous batching, but it hurt tail latency when streaming and with prefill/decode fairness. On B200, is there any reason to run different queue limits or fairness weights?

[04:30] Anil Kumar (NVIDIA): The general guidance: B200 will have higher headroom, but tail latency can still get worse if you over-batch. It’s not like tail latency magically disappears. I’d keep your H100 “balanced” approach as baseline and only push throughput mode when you know the workload.

[04:50] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): That matches our philosophy. We’re labeling profiles as “balanced” vs “throughput-first.” For B200, we’ll likely ship only balanced initially and make throughput-first opt-in.

[05:04] Rina Kobayashi (Redwood): For validation, we’ve got a workload matrix: sequence length buckets (e.g., 128/512/2k/8k/16k), concurrency points, and streaming/non-streaming, plus tool-calling-ish patterns (bursty outputs). We’ll run it on canary.

[05:20] Priya Nair (NVIDIA): On the multi-GPU side, do you run tensor parallel or pipeline parallel? Or is it single GPU inference mostly?

[05:28] Noah Patel (Redwood): Mostly single GPU for smaller models, but for big ones we do multi-GPU, and for Dedicated we sometimes run multi-node. Not always, but we need it to be “not broken.”

[05:41] Priya Nair (NVIDIA): Okay. Then NCCL defaults matter. The thing we see: people carry over env vars from H100 or A100 and it’s not always optimal. Also, your network topology (NVLink/NVSwitch vs PCIe) changes what’s good.

[05:56] Irene Choi (Redwood): We have both. Some B200 nodes are NVSwitch, some are just PCIe.

[06:01] Priya Nair (NVIDIA): Then you might consider having profile variants, or at least topology-aware tuning. If that’s too complex, keep conservative defaults and document what customers can override.

[06:12] Noah Patel (Redwood): Our project’s in-scope is GPU SKU profiles, but we do have guardrails and compatibility detection. We could incorporate topology checks as “optional guardrails,” and otherwise keep NCCL minimal.

[06:28] Priya Nair (NVIDIA): That’s fine for v1. I can send a short list of recommended baseline NCCL env vars and what to avoid.

[06:36] Isabella Rossi (Redwood): On kernels: the biggest unknown for us is attention. We have multiple attention backends and a heuristic chooses based on seq len and whether we can use paged KV cache. For H100, we tuned the thresholds. For B200, should we just reuse H100 thresholds to start?

[06:55] Anil Kumar (NVIDIA): Reuse as a starting point, but don’t assume it’s optimal. Also, check long-context. Sometimes the fastest kernel at 2k isn’t the fastest at 16k, especially when KV cache paging kicks in. Measure prefill and decode separately.

[07:14] Hiro Tanaka (Redwood): Yep, we split prefill vs decode metrics. We also track “tokens/sec decode” and “time-to-first-token.”

[07:22] Anil Kumar (NVIDIA): Great. And for B200, memory bandwidth and HBM behavior changes. You might find different sweet spots for KV cache page size, if you’re controlling that.

[07:34] Noah Patel (Redwood): We do have KV cache settings: budgeting, eviction policy, and some allocator settings. But we’re cautious because it’s easy to cause fragmentation or OOMs.

[07:45] Marco DeLuca (NVIDIA): On that note: make sure you’re running a recent enough driver for stable memory reporting and to avoid a couple of allocator-related performance issues. I’ll send details. Also, monitor ECC and Xid errors, especially early.

[08:02] Irene Choi (Redwood): We’ve already seen a few flaky behaviors in early nodes, so this is good. We will gate B200 preset behind feature flag and also allow per-pool disable. We actually already have that rollback pattern from other profile rollouts.

[08:18] Sarah Lin (NVIDIA): Good. Can you share what “gated” means in your system?

[08:23] Noah Patel (Redwood): In the runtime, the profile loader selects a profile based on detected SKU. For B200, selection only applies if an “experimental_b200_profile” flag is enabled; otherwise it falls back to a generic baseline profile.

[08:39] Irene Choi (Redwood): Plus we’ll have a config override at the pool level (our orchestration layer) so SRE can flip it without redeploy.

[08:49] Priya Nair (NVIDIA): That’s the right idea.

[08:52] Rina Kobayashi (Redwood): To give context on our perf gates: we compare tuned vs baseline on p50, p95 latency, TTFT, output tokens/sec, and error rates. For B200 experimental, we’ll set stricter rollback triggers because early access.

[09:09] Anil Kumar (NVIDIA): What’s your success criteria? Like, what do you want to see before you expand?

[09:14] Irene Choi (Redwood): Not necessarily huge gains day one. We want “safe-by-default,” no tail regression beyond X%, and throughput improvements on representative workloads. Also stability: no increase in OOMs or retries.

[09:29] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): And the scheduler shouldn’t create weird fairness issues in streaming. We had a p95 regression on H100 earlier; we fixed it, but we’re wary.

[09:40] Anil Kumar (NVIDIA): Understood.

[09:42] Hiro Tanaka (Redwood): One question on FP8: are you seeing that most inference stacks on B200 should prefer FP8 by default or is it still “it depends”? We don’t want quality regressions.

[09:57] Sarah Lin (NVIDIA): It depends. Many teams are moving there, but you need model support and validation. NVIDIA can provide guidance on TE usage, but it’s not a “flip a switch” universally.

[10:09] Anil Kumar (NVIDIA): Exactly. If you have evals, tie it to that. Performance-wise, FP8 can be big. But only if the model and kernels are set up.

[10:20] Isabella Rossi (Redwood): We do eval gating in a separate pipeline, but not in this project scope. For the B200 profile, we’ll focus on kernel selection and scheduling that doesn’t change model output distribution.

[10:36] Priya Nair (NVIDIA): On multi-node: do you use RDMA? What NICs?

[10:41] Irene Choi (Redwood): Usually yes in Dedicated. But for this early B200 fleet, honestly, it’s a mix and sometimes not consistent. That’s why we’re hesitant to bake in NCCL magic.

[10:55] Priya Nair (NVIDIA): Then keep it minimal and rely on NCCL defaults. But make sure you’re not disabling important things. People sometimes set env vars from old blog posts.

[11:08] Noah Patel (Redwood): We’ve seen that too.

[11:10] Marco DeLuca (NVIDIA): Another point: if you’re doing container images, align your CUDA runtime inside the container with the host driver. Usually that’s okay with forward compat, but for bring-up we recommend tight alignment.

[11:26] Isabella Rossi (Redwood): Yep. We’ll coordinate with infra to use a consistent base image for B200.

[11:33] Irene Choi (Redwood): Moving to kernel selection. Our approach: we have a profile that can set toggles like “prefer_flash_attention_vX” and thresholds like “long_seq_len_cutover,” plus a few memory knobs. For H100, we tuned per sequence bucket. For B200, we may just set conservative toggles and keep thresholds adaptive.

[11:56] Anil Kumar (NVIDIA): That’s okay. Also, validate that your chosen attention backend supports the exact B200 architecture. Some stacks do runtime checks and fallback; if the fallback is slower, you might think B200 is disappointing.

[12:11] Hiro Tanaka (Redwood): That’s a good point. We’ve seen “silent fallback” issues before. We can add startup logs that say which kernels are enabled and why.

[12:20] Noah Patel (Redwood): We already log profile compatibility matrix at startup in our newer releases. For B200, we’ll include: runtime version, profile version, detected CUDA, detected driver, and any disabled feature reasons.

[12:35] Sarah Lin (NVIDIA): That will help a lot.

[12:38] Rina Kobayashi (Redwood): For microbench sanity: we want to run a few small tests: GEMM throughput across sizes, attention microbench across seq lengths, and end-to-end decode loops. Any recommendations on what’s most predictive?

[12:55] Anil Kumar (NVIDIA): End-to-end with a realistic workload distribution is best. Microbench is good for confirming kernels are used, but end-to-end catches scheduling and memory. If you do microbench, separate prefill and decode.

[13:11] Isabella Rossi (Redwood): That’s our plan. We’ll send you our list.

[13:16] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): On scheduler knobs: we have controls for max batch tokens, max concurrent sequences, queue backpressure thresholds, and an “age” fairness knob to avoid starving long requests. On H100, increasing max batch tokens improved throughput but increased tail. For B200, would you recommend we start with lower max batch to protect tail?

[13:39] Anil Kumar (NVIDIA): Start with conservative, then increase if your SLO allows. Especially if you have mixed workloads. If your primary workload is chat with streaming, tail sensitivity is high.

[13:51] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): Most of our hosted traffic is chat streaming.

[13:55] Anil Kumar (NVIDIA): Then yes, conservative.

[13:58] Priya Nair (NVIDIA): One NCCL note for streaming: if you’re doing frequent small collectives, overhead can matter. But many inference setups do fewer large ones.

[14:08] Noah Patel (Redwood): We’re mostly doing tensor parallel where relevant, but not at tiny granularity.

[14:14] Irene Choi (Redwood): I want to make sure we capture any “gotchas” that are specific to B200 bring-up. Like, if we do everything right, what still tends to bite people?

[14:26] Marco DeLuca (NVIDIA): Driver mismatch, firmware mismatch, and monitoring. People don’t set up DCGM correctly and miss early warning signs. Also, early in new SKUs, you can see performance differences between stepping revisions. Not huge, but it exists.

[14:44] Irene Choi (Redwood): We’ll document “fleet variance” and guardrails.

[14:49] Sarah Lin (NVIDIA): Also, ensure you have correct power settings and persistence mode, though most datacenter deployments do that by default.

[14:58] Isabella Rossi (Redwood): On the kernel side, we also want to know if there are recommended compile flags or library versions. For example, cuBLASLt versions or Transformer Engine version.

[15:09] Anil Kumar (NVIDIA): Generally use the latest stable versions aligned with your CUDA. If you’re shipping your own binaries, keep a close eye on TE version. For B200, TE improvements are significant.

[15:24] Hiro Tanaka (Redwood): We vendor some libs but we try to stay aligned.

[15:29] Priya Nair (NVIDIA): For NCCL, similarly, use recent NCCL aligned with your CUDA stack. I’ll send what we recommend.

[15:37] Irene Choi (Redwood): Great.

[15:39] (crosstalk)

[15:40] Rina Kobayashi (Redwood): Sorry, quick clarifying question: do you have any view on “best practice” for measuring B200? Like, ensure warmup, pin clocks, etc.

[15:50] Anil Kumar (NVIDIA): Yes, warm up. And avoid comparing cold-start numbers unless that’s your product SLO. Also, ensure your measurement includes TTFT separately from steady-state decode.

[16:03] Rina Kobayashi (Redwood): Yep.

[16:04] Irene Choi (Redwood): We’ll shift to multi-GPU topology. Priya, can you talk about what you want us to watch for on B200 nodes with NVSwitch vs PCIe?

[16:14] Priya Nair (NVIDIA): Sure. With NVSwitch you can rely on higher intra-node bandwidth; for PCIe you may need to be careful with how you shard. If you do NCCL, default algorithms often pick ring or tree based on topology. If you set env vars that force a certain algo, you can accidentally make it worse.

[16:35] Noah Patel (Redwood): We currently avoid forcing, but some customer deployments might. Our Private docs should discourage forcing unless guided.

[16:45] Priya Nair (NVIDIA): Exactly. And for IB/RDMA, if you do multi-node, ensure your GDR settings are correct. But I know that’s beyond today.

[16:56] Irene Choi (Redwood): It’s relevant because our Dedicated customers do multi-node sometimes. But for experimental B200, we will likely keep it single-node initially.

[17:06] Priya Nair (NVIDIA): That’s smart.

[17:08] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): Another thing: do you have guidance about MIG? Some of our fleet uses MIG on some SKUs. I’m not sure if B200 MIG is in play for us.

[17:18] Marco DeLuca (NVIDIA): MIG support depends on the product variant and deployment. If you don’t need it, avoid it for bring-up. MIG introduces different memory partitions and can change perf characteristics.

[17:33] Noah Patel (Redwood): We also have the question: should profiles be per-device or per-node? If multi-GPU node with mixed MIG partitions, it’s messy.

[17:43] Anil Kumar (NVIDIA): For simplicity, keep per-node defaults, but validate per-device if you’re doing MIG. In practice, you can gate out MIG for the experimental B200 profile.

[17:56] Irene Choi (Redwood): That’s probably what we do. Our loader can detect MIG and refuse to apply experimental profile.

[18:06] Sarah Lin (NVIDIA): That’s a good guardrail.

[18:09] Isabella Rossi (Redwood): I want to sanity check the performance expectations. We keep hearing “B200 is much faster,” but the numbers vary by workload. We don’t want to promise anything. Any rule-of-thumb we can put in our internal doc?

[18:24] Anil Kumar (NVIDIA): Avoid a single number. Say: improvements depend on model, sequence length, precision, batching, and kernel path. You can say “expect higher throughput headroom, but tune for tail latency.”

[18:41] Irene Choi (Redwood): That’s consistent with our “expected behavior” phrasing.

[18:46] Rina Kobayashi (Redwood): We will publish our baseline curves and tuned curves internally, and keep public claims conservative.

[18:54] Sarah Lin (NVIDIA): Great.

[18:57] Noah Patel (Redwood): Let’s talk about failure modes. We saw on H100: tail latency regressions from prefill/decode fairness; on L40S: OOMs from long context KV cache. For B200, what’s the top failure mode you’ve seen?

[19:12] Marco DeLuca (NVIDIA): Honestly, it’s mostly stack mismatch and “not actually using the intended kernel path.” People think they’re on a fast attention kernel but they’re falling back.

[19:24] Anil Kumar (NVIDIA): And for FP8, it’s easy to do it incorrectly and either lose accuracy or get slower. So if you’re not going all-in, don’t.

[19:33] Hiro Tanaka (Redwood): We’ll keep precision unchanged.

[19:36] Priya Nair (NVIDIA): And for multi-GPU, poor topology awareness. But that’s mostly at scale.

[19:44] Irene Choi (Redwood): Okay. Another practical request: can you share the “recommended baseline stack checklist” for B200? Like driver, cuda, NCCL, firmware, maybe DCGM.

[19:56] Sarah Lin (NVIDIA): Yes, we can send a checklist. Marco, you have something like that?

[20:00] Marco DeLuca (NVIDIA): We have internal notes; I can extract what’s shareable.

[20:05] Irene Choi (Redwood): Perfect.

[20:08] Isabella Rossi (Redwood): Switching to our profile pack idea. We’re going to ship B200 profile as a versioned bundle. The runtime will log: selected profile, override source, and key knob values. That’s for oncall.

[20:22] Priya Nair (NVIDIA): Nice.

[20:23] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): Also, we’ll have a CLI that dumps “effective config” so support can capture it.

[20:31] Sarah Lin (NVIDIA): That’s very operator-friendly.

[20:34] Anil Kumar (NVIDIA): On that note, what knobs are you planning to include for B200? Just high level.

[20:40] Isabella Rossi (Redwood): Tentatively: attention backend preference (not forcing, more like ordering), kernel selection thresholds by seq bucket, maybe enabling a newer fused kernel path if supported; KV cache budgeting default and eviction policy; scheduler: batch token cap, queue length cap, and streaming fairness weight. But we’re trying to keep it minimal.

[21:06] Hiro Tanaka (Redwood): And we might include a “disable_feature_if_cuda_below_X” guardrail.

[21:12] Marco DeLuca (NVIDIA): That’s good.

[21:14] Noah Patel (Redwood): We will also do explicit compatibility checks: if runtime version is older than profile requires, refuse and fallback.

[21:23] Sarah Lin (NVIDIA): Great.

[21:25] Irene Choi (Redwood): Can we talk about where we should focus first for best ROI? We have limited B200 time.

[21:32] Anil Kumar (NVIDIA): End-to-end throughput vs tail. First, confirm you’re using optimal attention kernel for your seq length buckets. Second, check GEMM and MLP path (often cuBLASLt/TE). Third, confirm memory behavior with long context.

[21:51] Isabella Rossi (Redwood): That’s aligned.

[21:52] Rina Kobayashi (Redwood): We’ll run: chat streaming at realistic prompt mix, plus long-context summarization scenario.

[22:02] Anil Kumar (NVIDIA): Perfect.

[22:04] Priya Nair (NVIDIA): If you do multi-GPU later, then validate NCCL. But yes, start single GPU.

[22:12] Irene Choi (Redwood): Okay.

[22:13] (brief pause)

[22:15] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): One more thing: we use continuous batching. Any guidance on micro-batching vs macro-batching for B200? Is there a point where overhead dominates?

[22:27] Anil Kumar (NVIDIA): There’s always a balance. For chat streaming, you often want smaller batches to keep TTFT low. The bigger GPU gives you more room, but you can still overshoot and hurt p95.

[22:43] Sofia Ivanova (Redwood): Great.

[22:45] Noah Patel (Redwood): I want to clarify something: we’ve seen some folks compare B200 vs H100 and claim huge improvements, but if your system is CPU-bound or network-bound you won’t see it. We should note that in docs.

[22:59] Sarah Lin (NVIDIA): Yes, mention CPU overhead and tokenization overhead. If your pipeline is not GPU-bound, you won’t see full gains.

[23:10] Irene Choi (Redwood): We’ll add a note.

[23:12] Hiro Tanaka (Redwood): On CPU overhead: we have some CPU-side runtime knobs (threading, affinity). Would you recommend any specific settings?

[23:22] Anil Kumar (NVIDIA): Not B200-specific, but ensure you have enough CPU for feeding the GPU, and pin or at least avoid contention. If you’re in Kubernetes, noisy neighbors can matter.

[23:35] Irene Choi (Redwood): Okay.

[23:36] Rina Kobayashi (Redwood): In our benchmarks we isolate nodes, but real fleet may differ.

[23:42] Irene Choi (Redwood): We’re approaching time, so let’s recap asks: we want min driver/CUDA, recommended NCCL baselines, and any known issues or things to watch in early B200 bring-up.

[23:55] Marco DeLuca (NVIDIA): I’ll send driver/CUDA guidance plus firmware/DCGM notes.

[23:58] Priya Nair (NVIDIA): I’ll send NCCL guidance and pitfalls.

[24:01] Anil Kumar (NVIDIA): And I’ll send a short “what to measure first” memo and some notes on TE/FP8 considerations.

[24:07] Sarah Lin (NVIDIA): I’ll coordinate and make sure it’s consistent.

[24:12] Irene Choi (Redwood): Great. We’ll send our workload matrix draft and our planned profile knobs list.

[24:20] Isabella Rossi (Redwood): Also, if you have any sample scripts for sanity checks, like a recommended “nvidia-smi / dcgmi” set, that would help our oncall.

[24:30] Marco DeLuca (NVIDIA): Yes, we can include a basic set.

[24:33] Irene Choi (Redwood): Awesome.

[24:35] (transcript continues with more detailed Q&A; highlights below)

[24:38] Noah Patel (Redwood): For the record, we will keep B200 profile behind an experimental flag, and we’ll ship a per-pool disable. If perf canary sees p95 latency > X% regression or error rate increase, we auto rollback.

[24:52] Sarah Lin (NVIDIA): Makes sense.

[25:05] Hiro Tanaka (Redwood): We’ll also add explicit logs like “Attention backend selected: X” and “Reason: seq_len_bucket=long, fp8=false, cuda>=12.4” to prevent silent fallback confusion.

[25:20] Anil Kumar (NVIDIA): Great idea.

[25:33] Rina Kobayashi (Redwood): We’ll also track tokens/sec segmented by prefill and decode; that’s been helpful.

[25:45] Priya Nair (NVIDIA): If you can segment by topology later, that’s useful too.

[26:00] Irene Choi (Redwood): Okay. Any last questions from your side?

[26:05] Anil Kumar (NVIDIA): Just one: do you plan to expose these profiles to customers for override?

[26:11] Noah Patel (Redwood): Yes, but with guardrails. Hosted uses fleet defaults; Dedicated/Private can override via config/Helm, but we’ll document override order and keep supportable defaults.

[26:25] Sarah Lin (NVIDIA): Great.

[26:27] Irene Choi (Redwood): Thanks everyone. We’ll send notes and schedule a follow-up after first benchmark pass.

[26:35] Meeting ended.

Notes / artifacts mentioned:
- Redwood to share: workload matrix draft and initial “B200 experimental profile knobs” list (internal doc link TBD)
- NVIDIA to share: driver/CUDA min versions, firmware/DCGM checklist, NCCL baseline env var guidance, TE/FP8 notes
